name: Zane Walsh

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time, Zane. I'm from the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We don't work for any company, union or party, and nothing you say will be linked to your name. Could you start by walking me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Sure. I'm a buyer at Harwick Fresh, a produce distributor that supplies about four hundred restaurants and corner grocers. My day starts at six with the overnight sales numbers, then I'm on the phone to growers and importers locking in tomatoes, citrus, salad leaves, whatever's short. By ten the trucks are booked and I'm arguing about price with a melon importer who always says the boat was late.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you like about it, and what wears you out?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I like the puzzle, honestly. Weather in one country changes what a chef in our city pays for lemons next week, and I'm the person in the middle making it work. What wears me out is the waste, throwing out two pallets of strawberries because I guessed wrong. I already run my forecasts through an AI model every morning, and it's better than my gut on most lines.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Here's the card: “Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.”

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Okay. Funny, because some days the tools I use already feel like more than hype, but I can picture it stalling.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At work I'd probably say, told you so, it's a fancy spreadsheet. With friends I'd be more honest and say it helped me cut waste a bit and that's about it. Online I'd post something about how the money would've been better spent on actual people.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, it means my job stays pretty much the same, which is fine. I'm well paid for a buyer, I've got more than a year of savings and there are other distributors all over the city. Mostly I'd be relieved for the warehouse crew, who were always the ones people joked about replacing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep using the forecasting model, because even small savings on spoilage count. I'd push my manager, Dana, to put the money we saved toward the night pickers' pay. I'd keep putting a fifth of my pay into savings like I do now, and probably take the Spanish class I keep putting off for the importer calls.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, mostly. A little bored at the idea, if I'm honest, because I like new things. But calm.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You mentioned the warehouse crew. Who would you actually be thinking about?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Raf on the night shift, mainly. He's been picking orders for nineteen years, and every time a new scanner comes in he gets nervous. In this picture Raf keeps his job and I'm glad.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anything that would still bother you, even with AI stalling?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The waste would still bother me. Even with the model, a bad week means pallets of berries in the skip. Hype or no hype, binning four percent of the fresh food we buy is the problem I'd want solved.

say: I'd say AI turned out to be a **fancy spreadsheet** that trimmed a bit of waste.
I'd argue the money spent on hype should have gone to **warehouse pay** instead.
think: My **buying job** stays the same, and with good pay and savings that feels fine.
I'm mostly relieved for the **warehouse crew**, who always got the replacement jokes.
do: Keep running the **forecasting model** each morning to cut spoilage on fresh lines.
Push my manager to put **spoilage savings** toward the night pickers' pay.
Keep saving a **fifth of my pay** and finally start the Spanish class.
feel: Mostly **calm**, with a touch of **boredom** because I like trying new things.
S0.quote: Hype or no hype, binning four percent of the fresh food we buy is the problem I'd want solved.
fieldNote: Zane already uses AI daily and treats a stall as **mildly disappointing**, not a relief for himself.
His first thought goes to **other workers**, especially Raf on the night shift.
He frames AI as a tool for **cutting food waste**, which he cares about more than speed.

steps.text: Keep running the produce forecast model every morning before supplier calls
Keep saving a fifth of each paycheck into the savings account

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Here's the card: “Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.”

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Right. That one sounds like next Tuesday, to be honest. Buying is literally on the list.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At work I'd say, look, we can use this to stop binning food and get better prices, but we need a say in how it's rolled out. To friends I'd say the buyers are first in line, and I'm one of them. Online I'd share stuff about office workers organising, because nobody in our office is in a union and the warehouse lads are.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I think the team of six buyers becomes three within a couple of years. I'm probably one of the three, because I already run the tools and I train the others on them. But I'd be keeping my job by helping make the other buyers redundant, and I'm not comfortable with that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: First month, I'd ask Dana to make me the person who sets up the new buying system, so I'm shaping it, not just using it. I'd book a supply chain analytics course, the evening one at the college, about two thousand to cover. And I'd talk to the warehouse union rep about whether office staff can join, because three buyers being cut quietly is exactly how it happens.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. I think I'm fine, but I'd be fine in a room where people I like aren't. That sits badly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd be fine while others aren't. Who on the buying team comes to mind?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Priyanka, mostly. She's brilliant with growers, she knows every farmer's kid's name, but she hates screens. If the job turns into checking what the system ordered, she's in trouble and she knows it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to your partner about it that night?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell Ruth, she teaches at the primary school, that I'm safe for now and I feel guilty about it. She'd tell me to stop being a martyr and go to the union meeting. She'd be right.

say: I'd say the tools can **cut waste**, but staff need a say in the rollout.
I'd tell friends **buyers are first** in line, and I'm one of them.
Online I'd back **office workers organising**, since only the warehouse is in a union.
think: I expect the **six buyers** to become three within a couple of years.
I'd probably stay, but by helping make **colleagues redundant**, which feels wrong.
do: Ask my manager to let me **set up the system** so I shape it.
Book the evening **supply chain analytics** course, about two thousand to cover.
Ask the warehouse **union rep** whether office staff can join.
feel: **Uneasy**, because I expect to be fine while people I like aren't.
A bit **guilty** about being the one who trains the system.
S1.quote: I'd be keeping my job by helping make the other buyers redundant, and I'm not comfortable with that.
fieldNote: Zane expects his **own job to survive** because he already runs the tools.
His unease is about **colleagues like Priyanka**, not his own income.
He turns quickly to **organising**, asking whether office staff can join the warehouse union.

steps.text: Volunteer to set up the new buying system at Harwick Fresh
Enrol in the evening supply chain analytics course at the college
Ask the warehouse union rep about letting buyers and office staff join

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Here's the card: “Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.”

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Two years. Okay. That's my job, basically, gone before my thirtieth birthday.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At work I'd say we need to sit down now and agree how people get paid out and retrained, before the board decides it for us. To friends I'd say this is exactly why we need a proper safety net, not just good intentions. Online I'd be loud about taxing the companies selling this stuff.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, a buyer is a person who reads numbers and talks to suppliers, and AGI does both. My savings would cover about fourteen months, which is more than most, but that's not a plan. The trucks, the forklifts and the pickers would keep going for another three years, and I'd be watching from the outside.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Right away I'd move my savings out of the general account into something boring and safe, so it lasts. I'd spend the first year getting closer to the physical side: spending days at the farms and the cold store, learning food safety and quality checking, things you have to stand in a field to do. And I'd join whatever union or campaign is pushing for a wage guarantee, because I'm not going to fight this alone.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. I've got more cushion than most, and I'm young, but I'd be one of the first to go and I know it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said robots come three years later. What does that gap mean for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It means the hands-on people get three more years and the desk people don't. I'd try to move toward the hands-on end, quality checks on arrival, cold chain, that kind of thing. It's not forever, but three years is a long time when you're twenty-seven.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you cut first, if you had to?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The trip Ruth and I were saving for, probably. We'd been planning six weeks travelling next summer. I'd rather hold that money than spend it on a beach while my job disappears.

say: I'd say staff and bosses must **agree payouts and retraining** before the board decides alone.
I'd argue this proves we need a **proper safety net** and taxes on AI companies.
think: AGI does both halves of buying, **reading numbers** and **suppliers**.
My **fourteen months of savings** is more than most, but it isn't a plan.
do: Move savings into a **safe, boring account** so they last longer.
Spend the first year learning **quality checks** and cold chain work at farms and the cold store.
Join a **union or campaign** pushing for a wage guarantee.
feel: **Anxious**, because I'd be among the **first to go**, even with savings.
S2.quote: A buyer is a person who reads numbers and talks to suppliers, and AGI does both.
fieldNote: Zane names his own job as **gone within two years** without hesitation.
He uses the **three-year robot gap** to plan a move toward hands-on quality work.
His savings give him **some control**, so he plans rather than panics.

steps.text: Move savings into a fixed-rate account so they last longer
Train in produce quality checks and cold chain handling at the cold store
Join the union campaign for a wage guarantee for replaced workers
Postpone the six-week trip with Ruth and keep the money

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Here's the card: “Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.”

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years. That's 2031 for the thinking work and 2034 for the robots. I'd be thirty-two when it lands.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At work I'd say we've got five years, let's use them, and I'd mean it. With friends I'd say five years is enough time to build something if governments start now. Online I'd keep pushing for public retraining money, because a course I can afford isn't one Raf can.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, five years means I can choose where to land instead of being thrown. Buying goes in 2031 whatever I do. The question is whether I spend the next five years squeezing out pay rises or setting up the next thing, and I think it's the second.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In the first year I'd do the analytics course and then something on food safety auditing, which needs someone on site. I'd start talking to two of our growers about helping them sell direct to restaurants, because they trust me and they'll need someone who knows both sides. And I'd still join the union push, because five years goes quickly if nobody's planning.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Still anxious, but it's a different kind. More like before an exam you've had time to study for.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd help growers sell direct. Wouldn't that cut out your own employer?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yeah, it would, and I'd have to be honest with Dana about it. But if AGI is running the buying in 2031, the distributor shrinks anyway. With five years' warning I'd rather be helping the farmers sell direct than defending a buying job that's going.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell Raf, with five years' warning?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell Raf to get his forklift and cold store tickets now, while the company still pays for training. The robots come later for his work, but they come. Five years is time to get every certificate he can.

say: I'd tell colleagues we have **five years** and should use them properly.
I'd push for **public retraining money**, since a course I can afford isn't one Raf can.
think: **Buying ends in 2031** whatever I do, so the question is where I land.
I'd rather spend five years **building the next thing** than chasing pay rises.
do: Finish the analytics course, then train in **food safety auditing**.
Start helping two growers **sell direct** to restaurants.
Keep pushing the **union campaign** for planned retraining.
feel: Still **anxious**, but more like **a studied exam** than a shock.
S3.quote: With five years' warning I'd rather be helping the farmers sell direct than defending a buying job that's going.
fieldNote: Zane treats five years as **a choice of landing**, not a reprieve.
He is willing to **compete with his employer** and plans to tell his manager.
His advice to Raf shows he thinks about **hands-on workers' later deadline**.

steps.text: Train as a food safety auditor after the analytics course
Help two local growers start selling direct to restaurants
Keep organising for a funded retraining plan with the union

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fifth and last picture is called AGI by 2036. Here's the card: “Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.”

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years. 2036 for the thinking AI, 2039 for robots. I'd be thirty-seven and forty. That's a whole career change with room to spare.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At work I'd say this is the version where nobody has an excuse, we've got a decade, so let's build the plan with staff, not around them. With friends I'd say it's the same ending, just with time to be decent about it. Online I'd keep pushing for the same things, just with less panic in my voice.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, ten years is a gift for someone my age. I can finish learning, build up the direct-sales work with the growers, and maybe even have kids with Ruth knowing what's coming. The risk is that ten years feels so far away that people do nothing until year eight.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep doing the buying job well for now and keep saving. Over the first year I'd start the food safety auditing qualification part time and help one grower set up direct deliveries as a test. I'd also volunteer at the union to write up what a fair ten-year plan for buyers and warehouse staff looks like.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. I'm not scared for myself with that much time. I'm worried we'll waste it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You mentioned having kids with Ruth. Would this change that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not the yes or no, but the timing maybe. With ten years we could have a kid while I'm still on a good wage and have the new work going before it lands. Honestly, two years would make me hold off, ten wouldn't.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who do you think would waste the ten years?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Management, mostly, and some of us too. Our firm still runs the warehouse rota on a whiteboard, so ten years of warning could easily feel like forever to management. If they treat ten years like forever, Raf finds out in year nine and that's when I'd get angry.

say: I'd say a **decade of warning** means nobody has an excuse to skip planning with staff.
I'd call it the **same ending** with time to be decent about it.
think: Ten years is a **gift at my age** for learning and building new work.
The real risk is people **doing nothing** until year eight.
do: Keep buying well and **keep saving** while the job lasts.
Start the **auditing qualification** part time and test direct deliveries with one grower.
Volunteer to draft a **fair ten-year plan** with the union.
feel: **Uneasy**, not for myself, but about the time being **wasted**.
S4.quote: Our firm still runs the warehouse rota on a whiteboard, so ten years of warning could easily feel like forever to management.
fieldNote: With ten years Zane feels **personally secure** and turns to how others will fare.
His worry is **institutional delay**, especially management at Harwick Fresh.
Family plans like **having children** depend on the warning time, he says openly.

steps.text: Start a part-time food safety auditing qualification this year
Run a direct delivery trial for one grower's salad leaves
Draft a ten-year transition plan for buyers with the union
Keep saving a fifth of pay while still on a buyer's wage

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, easily. Not because of me, I'd land somewhere, but because Raf and Priyanka and half the office wouldn't. What would help is a guaranteed income for a couple of years after you're replaced, and retraining that's paid for, not a loan.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe who gets the money. Every version you read out, someone saves a fortune on wages, and if none of that money comes back to the workers it's a bad deal. I don't care how clever the AI is.

headlineQuote: Every version you read out, someone saves a fortune on wages, and if none of that money comes back to the workers it's a bad deal.
portrait: Zane is a 27-year-old **produce buyer** at Harwick Fresh who uses AI forecasting every morning.
He has **over a year** of savings, a partner who teaches, and plenty of other distributors nearby.
He expects buying to be among the **first desk jobs** to go and plans calmly for himself.
His feelings run highest about **colleagues and warehouse staff**, and he reaches for unions and public retraining.
With more warning he leans toward **hands-on food safety work** and helping growers sell direct.
biggestWorry: AGI by 2028 worries him most, because colleagues like Raf and Priyanka would have **no time to adjust**.
whatWouldHelp: A **guaranteed income** for a couple of years after replacement, plus **paid retraining** rather than loans.
